not generic permeability, toxicity, or a computational prediction.

Record cards expose source-native values under their original column names.
Missing source values are omitted; do not assume a hidden canonicalized value.


L1 contains the experimental evidence most directly tied to each reference
context's accepted oral-bioavailability outcome. Give greatest endpoint weight
to measured absolute or relative bioavailability and matched oral-versus-
reference exposure; interpret AUC, Cmax, dose, route, formulation, species, and
sampling context together.

L2 adds related experimental records for the same molecule and exact condition.
Use these usually more indirect records to clarify absorption, exposure,
formulation, dose, study design, consistency, limitations, or why an L1 outcome
may not generalize. Permeability, solubility, or mechanism alone is not a direct
oral-bioavailability outcome.


First determine what every measurement says about its reference molecule. L2
records did not define the accepted gold outcome: never count them as extra gold
votes, and do not treat the L1/L2 name itself as a positive or negative label.

Treat transfer_likelihood as one relevance signal for whether a reference
parent-condition context may apply to the query. It is not a positive-class
probability, an experimental result, or a substitute for reasoning about the
visible structure, endpoint, assay, species, formulation, exposure, and
condition. Infer direction from the record cards first, then judge transfer from
all visible context. Do not invent a numeric similarity judgment or assume that
a higher transfer_likelihood must outweigh a concrete experimental mismatch.

Use general medicinal-chemistry knowledge to interpret structures, but ground
every compound-specific empirical claim in the supplied query prior or cited
record cards. Repeated records and multiple cards from one context are not
independent evidence. Return exactly one valid JSON object and do not reveal
hidden chain-of-thought.

claims.claim: Mannitol, a small polar hexitol, has measured absolute oral bioavailability of 63% in healthy adult men and ~20-24% in colonoscopy patients at 50-150 g; L3 oral exposure records show dose-linear Cmax and AUC after oral mannitol, confirming that very polar polyols can be absorbed systemically.

Glucose and propylene glycol, other small polar molecules, show high oral bioavailability (glucose F 0.722-0.843 in humans and 70-100% OGTT estimates; propylene glycol very high/close to complete), and sorbitol shows F 0.36-0.38 in shunted patients, supporting F>=20% for polar small molecules.

L3 exposure records for D-ribose (5 g oral, AUC0-inf 53.1 µg·h/mL) and calcium L-threonate (2025 mg oral, Cmax 43.8 mg/L·h on day 1, tmax ~1.6 h) show that polar sugar/polyhydroxy acid molecules related to ascorbic acid achieve measurable systemic exposure after oral dosing.

Low-F records (gemcitabine ~10%, sorbitol zero in normal subjects, glucose low in ponies) are explained by first-pass metabolism/clearance or species-specific presystemic catabolism, not by poor absorption; ascorbic acid lacks the gemcitabine CDA liability and has active transport (SVCT1/2) noted in the prior.

The physicochemical prior's unfavorable passive permeability is uncertain; its own caveat notes active transport could significantly enhance absorption, and the empirical pattern of polar small molecules supports F>=20%.

evidence_gaps: No direct absolute oral bioavailability measurement for ascorbic acid is present in the supplied cards; all support is transfer-based.
L3 oral exposure records (Cmax/AUC) lack IV comparators and therefore do not by themselves quantify F.
Ascorbic acid absorption is dose-dependent via SVCT1/2; the F>=20% threshold may not hold at very high gram doses, but typical oral doses are not specified.
Sorbitol zero-F normal records show first-pass can dominate for polyols; relevance to ascorbic acid is uncertain without direct hepatic extraction data.
Some context cards have canonical SMILES mismatching the named drugs (frusemide, pipemidic acid, diflunisal), reducing transferability.
No formulation, dose, or species match for ascorbic acid is provided.
